A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-knockout experiments, layer-wise representation probes and VideoQA evaluations in Sections 3.2–3.5 and Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original multi-token generation, spatial-task, failure-case and cumulative-knockout analyses.

M1.justification: The models, basic Attention Knockout and Logit Lens operations, and effective-pathway selection rule remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds a limited adaptation of the analysis procedure: identifying verb anchors and tracing successive generation stages through previously generated response tokens.

E1.justification: v2 adds VCGBench Temporal QA for multi-token open-ended responses and Video-MME action-recognition and spatial-perception tasks. These substantially broaden the evaluated question and response requirements. TVBench, TOMATO and LongVideoBench were already evaluated in v1; long-video coverage itself is not new.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same ImageLLM counterparts and VideoLLMs. Table 3 still compares full causal attention, effective pathways and random blocking for the same four models. The added analyses introduce no new baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: New protocols include successive verb-generation probes, separate incorrect-answer tracing on failure samples, VideoLLaMA3-7B evaluation with 8 versus 24 frames on LongVideoBench, and progressively expanding prefix/suffix layer knockouts (Appendices B.2 and G.2–G.4). The original training recipes and principal evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds concept-localization analysis, attention-map case studies across additional tasks, multi-token routing analysis, frame-count sensitivity, spatial-versus-temporal comparisons, failure diagnostics and a cumulative signal-leakage check. These test substantially more questions about mechanisms and robustness. The original half-layer and window-size ablations remain.

E5.justification: Shaded bands already appear in v1's plots and are retained in v2. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests. The added plots and discussion of sample variance do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The original tabulated values remain unchanged: for example, Table 3 retains TVBench scores of 51.5 and 51.2 for LLaVA-NeXT-7B-Video-FT with full and effective attention. Substantial new results show increasing reliance on generated-response anchors, task-dependent cross-frame sensitivity, two failure profiles, concept localization and robustness under cumulative knockouts (Figures D, V–AB, 5 and 10).

T1.justification: Section 2.1 corrects the dimensional specification of standard attention: v1 groups the output projection with d × d_H projections, whereas v2 specifies per-head query/key/value projections and a d × d output projection. This is a limited mathematical correction; no new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same four central claims: early-to-middle cross-frame interaction, temporal-keyword integration, middle-to-late answer generation, and performance retention through effective pathways. The 58% attention-edge suppression example is unchanged. Added experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning spatial concepts stabilizing before temporal concepts occupy remaining tokens, dynamically emerging response checkpoints, erroneous temporal signals versus static-bias failures, and weaker visual dependence in some tasks. Section 4 and Appendix G.7 also add proposed applications and an explanation of late-layer probability increases.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the spaCy model used for verb extraction and adds a reproducibility statement describing the implementation's codebase and explicitly reporting model availability through the existing project page. Training hyperparameters, hardware, vocabulary lists and effective-layer selection details are retained from v1.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds a VideoQA-benchmark discussion, including TempCompass, Vinoground, TemporalBench and MotionBench. Section 4 adds references connecting the findings to regularization and early exit. The core positioning relative to existing multimodal mechanistic-interpretability research remains unchanged; bibliography corrections and relocation are not new research relationships.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the main exposition are rewritten. Related Work moves to Appendix A, a new Discussion occupies Section 4, and the appendices are reordered and subdivided, including separate single-token and multi-token analyses. Reproducibility, acknowledgments and LLM-use statements are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material for concept localization, multi-token generation, additional attention maps, failures, long-video and spatial analyses, and signal leakage. Existing plot images are retained but regrouped and relocated, including consolidated model-specific appendix pages. Several tables also receive revised widths and spacing.

improvement.justification: v1 concentrated on successful cases and constrained single-token completion, leaving important questions about generation, failures and knockout validity. v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through multi-token analysis, failure diagnostics, spatial-task comparisons and cumulative interventions (Appendix B.2, Section 4 and Appendices G.2–G.4), while preserving the original experiments. Some mechanistic explanations remain conjectural and statistical reporting is unchanged, but the added controls and diagnostics provide a substantial net improvement in the support and applicability of the conclusions.
